passage: Dolma, you asked why I never push you to tell me things. Sit. I am Sahil, and when I was ten I pushed a friend badly. Pema kept a folded paper in her pencil case, and she went quiet each time I came near. Every day I asked, "What is it? What are you hiding?" Finally she shut the lid and said, "Stop asking." My face felt hot. That night I thought about it. Next morning I said, "I'm here whenever you feel like talking. I won't ask again." And I didn't. Three weeks later, by the well, she showed me the paper herself. It was her mother's letter from the city. She said it was hers to share, and I never forgot that.

qa.q: What did Pema keep in her pencil case?
qa.a: A folded paper.

qa.q: What was Sahil feeling when Pema shut the lid and said "Stop asking"?
qa.a: Probably embarrassed and hurt, since his face felt hot and he kept thinking about it that night.

qa.q: What could a friend say instead of pressing for a secret?
qa.a: Say "I'm here if you want to talk," and then let it go without asking again.

qa.q: How might Pema have felt about being asked every day?
qa.a: Crowded and pressured, which could explain why she went quiet and told him to stop, though later she chose to share the paper herself.

grounding: An elder recalls repeatedly pressing a friend about what she hid, then offering to listen and letting it go so she could choose.

passage:
I was next to Uma at lunch on Thursday, so I saw how it went. Half the table was whispering about Nisha's family, something about her parents shouting at night. Uma leaned in so far her rice nearly tipped. She asked, "Who told you that?" Then Nisha walked past with her tray, head down, and Uma stopped chewing. She said, "Did anyone finish the maths sheet?" A girl tried to go back to the story, and Uma shrugged, "I don't want to say more." Later Kavita asked her to pass it on to the next class, and Uma said no. I honestly can't tell whether she was curious, guilty, or both.

- Jaya, Class 6

qa.q: What did Uma ask when she leaned in?
qa.a: She asked, "Who told you that?"

qa.q: What might Uma have been thinking when Nisha walked past with her head down?
qa.a: Uma stopped chewing and changed the subject, which suggests she may have felt uncomfortable or guilty, though Jaya says she can't tell for sure.

qa.q: What could Uma do if others keep pulling her back into the whispering?
qa.a: She can keep changing the topic, say she doesn't want to say more, and not pass anything on.

qa.q: How might Nisha be affected if she noticed the whispers?
qa.a: It would probably hurt to hear her family trouble whispered about, and she walked past with her head down. 😔

grounding: Everyone whispers about a girl's family trouble and the child is curious too, but listens less, changes the topic and does not pass it on, seen by a classmate.

passage: Kiara had laughed at Divyansh's drawing in front of the whole class, so at recess he whispered to Mohit that she copied her maths homework. Mohit grinned. It felt good, like winning a game. By afternoon the story had grown: now Kiara copied in exams too, and two girls stopped sharing their tiffin with her. Divyansh saw Kiara wiping her eyes near the water cooler, and his good feeling curdled. He tried telling Mohit, "It's not true, forget it," but Mohit had already told three others. "Too late, yaar." That evening Divyansh wondered why he hadn't simply told Kiara she had hurt him, or asked the class teacher for help.

qa.q: What did Divyansh whisper to Mohit at recess?
qa.a: That Kiara copied her maths homework.

qa.q: How did Divyansh's feelings change after he saw Kiara near the water cooler?
qa.a: His good feeling curdled: the quick satisfaction turned into regret when he saw her wiping her eyes.

qa.q: What could Divyansh have done instead of whispering about Kiara?
qa.a: He could have told Kiara directly that she had hurt him, or asked the class teacher for help.

qa.q: What is it like for Kiara after the story grew?
qa.a: She is upset over a story that isn't true, wiping her eyes while two girls stop sharing their tiffin with her.

grounding: A child spreads a rumour out of spite, gets quick satisfaction, sees it grow out of control, and realises telling her directly or asking a teacher was wiser.

passage: In the coat room in Bergen, Astrid heard two boys whisper, "That's the girl who stole from the art box." Her face went hot. By the second lesson, other children were looking at her sideways. She wanted to sink through the floor. At break she found Ingrid on the bench, and Ingrid said right away, "I know that's not true. Want to sit with me?" Astrid told her class teacher that afternoon, hands shaking, and the teacher said it wasn't her fault and that they would deal with it. Next day Astrid told the boy she had learned started it, "Please stop saying that. It isn't true." Her voice wobbled, but she said it.

qa.q: What did the boys whisper in the coat room?
qa.a: "That's the girl who stole from the art box."

qa.q: How was Astrid feeling when she wanted to sink through the floor?
qa.a: Exposed and ashamed even though the story was untrue, and her face went hot.

qa.q: What would you advise Astrid to do if the whispers keep going?
qa.a: Keep telling the class teacher, hold on to friends like Ingrid, and ask whoever started it to stop again.

qa.q: How might Ingrid see Astrid's situation?
qa.a: Ingrid knows it isn't true, so she sees an unfair rumour and wants Astrid not to be alone, which is why she offered a seat.

grounding: A child finds a rumour about her everywhere and feels exposed, then tells a trusted adult, asks the source to stop and leans on a friend who knows her.

passage: Rain hammered the tin shed at the bus stop, and twenty schoolchildren were squeezed under it. Chetan, shoulder to shoulder with Saurabh, was grinning. "Did you see Imran's shoes? Must be from a charity box." Two boys sniggered. Saurabh's stomach clenched. Imran had shared his umbrella with him last week. "That's not nice," Saurabh said. "He's not here to answer." Chetan rolled his eyes. "Relax." The talk moved on to Imran's lunch. Saurabh felt his ears burn. There was no room to move away, so he stepped out to the edge, where rain dripped down his collar, and watched the road for the bus, jaw tight.

qa.q: What did Chetan say about Imran's shoes?
qa.a: He said they must be from a charity box.

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling as Chetan talked about Imran, and why?
qa.a: Uneasy and protective: Imran had shared his umbrella with him last week, so the jokes bothered him.

qa.q: What could Saurabh do next time if the gossip continues?
qa.a: He could repeat that it isn't nice, change the subject, or step away as he did.

qa.q: How might Chetan see Saurabh's "That's not nice"?
qa.a: Chetan rolled his eyes and said "Relax," so he may see it as a fuss over a joke and not realise it stung.

grounding: Friends gossip about someone the child likes; he says it is not nice, does not join, and steps away when uneasy.

passage: At the corner of the Seoul schoolyard, Leila lowered her voice. "Come on, tell us what Yuna said about her grandmother's cooking. Everyone's laughing." Soo-ah's palms turned damp. If she said nothing, they might start whispering about her next. She had seen it happen to Mina last month. "I don't really have anything," she said, and smiled politely. Leila's eyes narrowed. "Boring." Soo-ah's heart thudded as she picked up her bag. "See you in class, Leila." Walking away, she felt shaky. In the library she noticed Hana, who always saved a seat for her without asking for anything. She sat down beside her.

qa.q: What did Leila want Soo-ah to tell them about?
qa.a: What Yuna said about her grandmother's cooking.

qa.q: What was Soo-ah afraid of when her palms turned damp?
qa.a: That if she said nothing, they might start whispering about her next, as she had seen happen to Mina.

qa.q: What would you advise Soo-ah about her friendship with Leila?
qa.a: Stay polite and out of the gossip, and spend time with kinder friends like Hana, since a friend who needs cruelty is not safe. 🙂

qa.q: How might Hana see Soo-ah's choice?
qa.a: Hana asks nothing of Soo-ah and saves her a seat, so she probably welcomes her and sees a friend who doesn't need gossip.

grounding: A child fears being gossiped about if she refuses to gossip, stays polite and out of it, and moves toward a kinder friend.

passage:
Monday. On the school steps Salma told two friends that Elizabeth had cheated in the spelling test, because Riya had said so. By the afternoon the whole class was repeating it.

Wednesday. Elizabeth sat with her head on her arms, crying, while a girl pointed. Then Salma overheard the teacher explaining that Elizabeth had simply re-taken the test after being ill. Salma's face burned. She had never checked.

Thursday. Salma found Elizabeth by the swings. "I repeated something that wasn't true, and I'm sorry." Then she went back to the same friends and said, "What I told you was wrong. She didn't cheat." Elizabeth wiped her cheeks. "Thanks for fixing it." Salma promised herself to check before repeating anything.

qa.q: What did Salma tell two friends on Monday?
qa.a: That Elizabeth had cheated in the spelling test.

qa.q: What was Salma feeling on Wednesday when she learned the truth?
qa.a: Guilt and shame: her face burned because she had never checked and Elizabeth was crying.

qa.q: How could Salma make the correction reach the people who heard the rumour?
qa.a: She can tell the same friends that what she said was wrong and that Elizabeth didn't cheat, as she does.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth have felt on Thursday when Salma apologised?
qa.a: Relieved and a little comforted, since she wiped her cheeks and said "Thanks for fixing it."

grounding: A child repeats something false, sees the girl cry, feels awful, and goes to say sorry and correct the rumour.

passage: Under the neem tree behind the village school, Pushpa giggled, "Have you heard? Divyansh cried at the temple fair when he lost his mother's hand, and a shopkeeper had to carry him home." The girls around the mid-day meal plates started laughing. Binita looked across the yard at Divyansh, alone, drawing lines in the dust with a stick. She remembered when her own slate broke and everyone laughed. Her chest tightened. "How would you feel if they said that about you?" she said quietly. Pushpa blinked. "Did anyone bring the skipping rope?" Binita added. The talk drifted. Later she sat near Divyansh and asked about his drawing.

qa.q: Where were the girls sitting when Pushpa told the story?
qa.a: Under the neem tree behind the village school.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling as she watched Divyansh, and what memory helped her?
qa.a: Sympathy and a tight chest, because she remembered when her own slate broke and everyone laughed.

qa.q: How could Binita help the talk move on kindly?
qa.a: She can ask quietly how the others would feel if it were said about them and then bring up something else, like the skipping rope.

qa.q: How might Divyansh feel when someone sits near him afterwards?
qa.a: He may feel less alone and glad that someone wants to talk about his drawing instead of the story.

grounding: A child imagines how it feels to be the talked-about one, asks what if it were about you, and kindly changes the subject.

passage: Alka, you said your friend keeps telling you stories about others. Listen to Bhupen's story. When I was eleven, a girl named Minu sat beside me and passed on the juiciest news every day: who failed, who fought at home. Then she would say, "Now you tell me something." At first I felt important. Then I noticed she never shared her own troubles, and she'd say, "I know something about you," with a little smile. I felt a small chill. I began to answer, "Nothing much," and kept my real news for my brother. She sulked, but I felt calmer. Friendship, I learned, should not feel like counting coins.

qa.q: What did Minu say after passing on the news?
qa.a: She would say, "Now you tell me something."

qa.q: What did Bhupen feel at first, and what changed?
qa.a: He first felt important, but then a small chill when he noticed Minu never shared her own troubles and hinted she knew something about him.

qa.q: What could Alka do if a friend keeps trading stories for secrets?
qa.a: Share less, stay careful, and keep real news for people she trusts, as Bhupen did with his brother.

qa.q: How might Minu have seen Bhupen's "Nothing much"?
qa.a: She sulked, so she probably felt she was losing the exchange she wanted.

grounding: A friend passes on stories and asks for secrets in return; the child notices it is about power, shares less and stays careful.

passage:
Monday. Yusuf told three classmates that Abhinav had been sent to the principal for stealing a pen. It wasn't true; he had only wanted to be the one with news.

Tuesday. "Yusuf, please stay after the bell," the teacher said. His mouth went dry. He thought of saying, "Not me." Instead he said, "I said it, and it wasn't true. I'm sorry." The teacher told him he would miss the next games period and that his parents would be told.

Wednesday. Missing games hurt. But Yusuf handed Abhinav a note: "Sorry for what I said." Abhinav read it twice and said, "Okay." Yusuf's shoulders dropped. He was not hiding any more.

qa.q: What did Yusuf tell three classmates?
qa.a: That Abhinav had been sent to the principal for stealing a pen.

qa.q: What was Yusuf thinking when his mouth went dry, and what did he decide?
qa.a: He was scared and thought of saying "Not me," but decided to admit it and apologise.

qa.q: Why was telling the truth the better choice for Yusuf?
qa.a: The consequences hurt, like missing games and his parents being told, but lying would have hurt more and kept him hiding.

qa.q: How might Abhinav have felt reading the note?
qa.a: He read it twice, so it likely mattered to him, though he only said "Okay," which suggests he may still be sorting out his feelings.

grounding: A teacher hears about a rumour and calls the child, who honestly says what he did and apologises, accepting the consequences.
